Best Kept Season

Why the Territory ↓
The Territory difference

It isn't empty. It's uncrowded.

Scroll for 20 things to know
01

Distances here run to hours, not minutes. Between towns you'll pass road trains, roadhouses, and more stars than you've ever seen.

02

Traditional Owners have cared for this land for over 65,000 years, the oldest continuous living culture on Earth.

03

Two seasons run the show: the Dry, from May to October, all blue sky, dust, and firelight evenings.

04

The Wet arrives November to April, when waterfalls roar back to life and the landscape turns green almost overnight.

05

Uluru changes colour through the day, from ochre at dawn to deep red at sunset, best watched in silence.

06

Kakadu spans nearly 20,000 square kilometres, home to ancient rock art, saltwater crocodiles, and wetlands thick with birdlife.

07

Kings Canyon's rim walk climbs steep sandstone early morning, rewarding hikers with views across an ancient, cracked plateau.

08

Litchfield's plunge pools sit close enough to Darwin for a day trip, yet feel worlds from the city.

09

Nitmiluk Gorge is best explored by canoe at first light, when the water is still and the walls glow.

10

Darwin's Mindil Beach markets run dry-season evenings, mixing food stalls, live music, and one of the world's best sunsets.

11

Alice Springs sits almost exactly at the continent's centre, a desert town ringed by the ancient MacDonnell Ranges.

12

Aboriginal-guided tours turn a landscape into a living story, sharing knowledge passed down for thousands of generations.

13

The Tanami and Sandover are proper outback tracks, best driven with fuel, water, and a plan you've shared with someone.

14

Barramundi fishing draws anglers to the Territory's rivers and coastlines, chasing one of Australia's most prized sportfish.

15

Night skies here are some of the darkest on Earth, with the Milky Way visible without any effort at all.

16

Termite mounds can stand taller than a person, some aligned north-south to regulate temperature through the desert heat.

17

The Ghan train crosses the Territory north to south, three days of red desert, tropical wetland, and everything between.

18

Bushfood and native ingredients, from wattleseed to Kakadu plum, are increasingly showcased on menus across Darwin and Alice Springs.

19

Crocodile spotting cruises on the Adelaide River are famous for saltwater crocodiles launching clear out of the water.

20

Whichever season you land in, the Territory rewards slowness: one long drive, one sunset, one gorge at a time.

Before you go

20 things worth knowing first.

Scroll for trip-planning basics
01

Fly into Darwin or Alice Springs, then decide whether you're chasing the Top End or the Red Centre.

02

Hire a car with decent clearance if you're leaving sealed roads, even for short detours off the highway.

03

Book Uluru sunrise or sunset viewing spots ahead in peak season, as the best pull-offs fill up fast.

04

Carry more water than feels necessary, especially on any walk longer than an hour in the heat.

05

Mobile signal drops out fast beyond towns, so download offline maps before you leave the last service station.

06

Fuel stops can be 200 kilometres apart, so fill up whenever the tank passes half, not when it's empty.

07

The Dry season, May to October, is the easiest time to visit, with mild days and almost no rain.

08

Wet season travel rewards flexibility, since some roads and gorges close after heavy rain without much warning.

09

Swimming isn't always safe up north, so check current advice on crocodiles before you jump into any water.

10

Pack layers even in the Dry, since desert nights drop close to freezing while days stay warm.

11

National park permits are required for some Aboriginal land, so check access rules before you plan a route.

12

A minimum of five days lets you properly cover either the Red Centre or Kakadu, not both at once.

13

Book Aboriginal-guided tours early, they offer context and stories a self-guided visit simply can't provide.

14

Sunscreen and a wide-brim hat matter more here than almost anywhere else you've likely travelled.

15

Accommodation ranges from outback stations to eco-camps, so book ahead in small towns during peak months.

16

The Ghan and long-distance coaches are relaxed alternatives to driving if you'd rather watch the country pass by.

17

Respect signage around sacred sites, some areas are closed to photography or climbing out of cultural respect.

18

Flies are relentless in the Dry, a simple head net makes walks noticeably more enjoyable.

19

Cash still works better than cards at remote roadhouses, where card readers and signal can be unreliable.

20

Tell someone your route and return time before any remote drive, and check in when you arrive.
